column1: # First-aid steps shown to the ambulance crew when they are dispatched.
# severity ANY = always shown; a specific severity adds steps after the general ones.
# SAMPLE CONTENT - have a doctor or paramedic review it before any real use.

column3: step
Little is known: check airway, breathing and pulse first.
Ask bystanders what happened and look for medicines or injuries.
Control any heavy bleeding with firm pressure.
If not breathing normally, start CPR and use the defibrillator.
Pre-alert the hospital emergency team.
Wear gloves and expose the wound.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or dressing.
If blood soaks through, add more pads on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first pad.
Keep the patient lying down and reassure them.
If an object is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out. Press around it.
Check pulse and breathing every 5 minutes.
For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, apply a tourniquet above the wound and note the time.
Treat for shock: keep the patient flat and warm, and raise the legs if there is no leg or spine injury.
Give oxygen and monitor pulse, blood pressure and consciousness continuously.
Pre-alert the hospital blood bank.
Wash the wound under running water with soap for 15 minutes.
Apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine.
Cover with a clean, loose dressing. Do not stitch or close the wound.
Note whether the dog is known, vaccinated or stray, for the rabies decision at the hospital.
If it is bleeding heavily, control the bleeding with firm pressure first.
Check for signs of shock and monitor pulse and breathing.
Keep the patient calm and still. Movement spreads venom faster.
Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint, like a fracture.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts.
Do NOT cut or suck the bite, apply ice, or tie a tight band around the limb.
Note the time of the bite and any symptoms for the doctor.
Monitor breathing, pulse and swelling every 5 minutes.
Give no injections into the muscle. Bleeding may be hard to stop.
Watch for drooping eyelids and weak breathing. Be ready to support breathing with a bag-valve-mask.
If the patient vomits, turn them onto their left side to protect the airway.
Pre-alert the hospital to prepare anti-snake venom and an ICU bed.
Note the exact time the symptoms started, or when the patient was last seen well.
Check FAST signs: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty.
Keep the head and shoulders slightly raised. Give nothing to eat or drink.
Check blood sugar. Low sugar can look like a stroke.
Give oxygen only if the oxygen level is below 94%.
If unconscious but breathing, place in the recovery position and protect the airway.
Pre-alert the hospital so the stroke team and CT scanner are ready on arrival.
Attach the monitor or defibrillator pads as early as possible.
Give oxygen and record pulse, blood pressure and oxygen level.
Keep the patient at rest, sitting up, and loosen tight clothing.
Record an ECG if available and send it to the hospital.
Give aspirin to chew if the local protocol allows and the patient is not allergic.
If not breathing normally, start CPR: 30 chest compressions to 2 breaths, 100-120 per minute, about 5-6 cm deep.
Use the defibrillator as soon as it is ready and follow its prompts.
Swap the person doing compressions every 2 minutes to keep CPR effective.
Pre-alert the hospital cardiac team and cath lab.
Check that the patient is breathing and responds to your voice.
Ask about medicines, allergies, recent food, alcohol or a fall.
Measure pulse, blood pressure, oxygen and blood sugar.
If unconscious but breathing, place in the recovery position.
If not breathing normally, start CPR and use the defibrillator.
Pre-alert the hospital emergency team.
Make the scene safe before approaching the patient.
Keep the head and neck still; assume a spine injury until ruled out.
Control bleeding with firm pressure.
Fit a cervical collar and move the patient on a spinal board.
Check airway, breathing and circulation every few minutes and give oxygen.
Pre-alert the hospital trauma team and blood bank.
Do not try to straighten the limb.
Support and splint the injured part in the position found.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling.
Cover an open wound with a clean dressing without pressing on the bone.
For hip, thigh or spine injuries move the patient on a spinal board and watch for shock.
Stop the burning: remove the patient from the heat source.
Cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice.
Remove rings and tight clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing.
Do not burst blisters or apply creams.
Give oxygen if smoke was inhaled and watch the airway closely.
Keep the patient warm to prevent hypothermia.
Sit the patient down in a comfortable position, half sitting.
Loosen tight clothing and keep the patient calm.
Record an ECG if available and monitor pulse and blood pressure.
Give aspirin to chew if not allergic, as per protocol.
Keep the defibrillator ready; start CPR if the patient stops breathing.
Pre-alert the hospital cath lab.
Sit the patient upright, leaning slightly forward.
Help the patient use their own inhaler if they have one.
Give oxygen and monitor oxygen levels.
Give nebulised medicine as per protocol.
Be ready to support breathing with a bag-valve mask.
Move hard or sharp objects away; do not hold the patient down.
Do not put anything in the mouth.
Note the time the fit started and how long it lasts.
After the fit, place the patient in the recovery position.
Check blood sugar and look for a head injury.
If the fit lasts more than 5 minutes, give anti-seizure medicine as per protocol and give oxygen.
Find out what was taken, how much and when; bring the container.
Do not make the patient vomit.
Check breathing and consciousness every few minutes.
Place an unconscious but breathing patient in the recovery position.
Support breathing and give oxygen; start CPR if breathing stops.
Pre-alert the hospital with the name of the substance.
Keep the patient on their side so they do not choke if they vomit.
Do not give more alcohol, coffee or a cold shower.
Check for injuries from falls and check blood sugar.
Monitor breathing closely; slow breathing is dangerous.
Support breathing and give oxygen; keep the patient warm.
Rest: stop the activity and do not use the injured part.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15 to 20 minutes.
Support with a compression bandage, not too tight.
Raise the injured part if possible.
Splint the part if it is out of shape and check the pulse below the injury.
Check blood sugar as soon as possible.
If sugar is low and the patient can swallow, give sugar, juice or glucose gel.
Do not give anything by mouth if the patient cannot swallow safely.
If sugar is very high, give fluids as per protocol and monitor breathing.
For an unconscious patient with low sugar, give glucose as per protocol and place in the recovery position.
